It solves the problem of overlapping data-value intervals in 1D transfer functions, where different materials or boundaries share similar scalar values but differ in their local structure [S4, book][S5, unofficial].

The claim states that the evidence supports the idea that a specific method (2D transfer functions using gradient magnitude) solves the problem of overlapping data-value intervals in 1D transfer functions, particularly where materials share similar scalar values but differ in local structure. Source [S4] explicitly states that 1D transfer functions are problematic due to 'overlap between the data-value intervals' and that multidimensional (2D) transfer functions using gradient magnitude 'discriminates between homogeneous regions... and regions of change' and allows features to be 'uniquely isolated'. It specifically mentions that the air-bone boundary cannot be isolated using a 1D function but can be with a 2D one. Source [S5] supports this by noting that 1D TFs cannot accurately capture all material boundaries (e.g., dentin vs background) and that 2D TFs provide greater flexibility in boundary visualization by mapping data value and gradient magnitude. Both sources confirm that adding gradient magnitude (local structure) allows the separation of materials with similar scalar values.
